A B S T R A C T
The metal cobalt is expected to be the next generation of interconnect materials due to its shorter average free
path of electrons and greater resistance to electromigration. Additives especially the leveling agents are key
regulatory factors for achieving a bottom-up dense superfilling of interconnect metals in the electroplating
process. Here the hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) with methylene structure was chosen as a leveling agent to
study the deposition behavior and the blind hole filling behavior of cobalt. The electrochemical analysis showed
that the HMTA exhibits an evident inhibition ability on the deposition of cobalt. Moreover, this inhibitory ability
has a significant dependence on the rotational speed of the solution and a greater inhibitory effect on the
deposition of cobalt occurs at high rotational speeds.The simulation indicates that such a strong inhibition ability
on the deposition of cobalt sourced from the preferred adsorption of the leveling agent on the cobalt surface by
the nucleophilic active site provided by the methylene structure of HMTA. Such preferential adsorption behavior
was further confirmed by the captured vibration peaks of C–N and C–H bonds associated with the HMTA from
the in-situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy. Under the action of this leveling agent, the
metal cobalt exhibits the expected bottom-up growth behavior in blind holes of Printed circuit board (PCB) The
addition of HMTA is also beneficial for obtaining a flat and dense coating with preferred growth of (100) crystal
planes. These results indicate that the HMTA is a potential effective leveling agent for the cobalt interconnects
processes.

recent researchers have mainly attempted to use accelerators used in the
damascus copper interconnect electroplating process as accelerators for

contain specific functional groups such as (-S-S-), thiols (-SH), and sul

concluded that the amide group of PVP and the thiol group of MPS may
be adsorption sites for cobalt electrodeposition. Four different sizes o
practical cobalt pillars were successfully electrodeposited through
electroplating experiments, thereby promoting the application of
metallic cobalt in electronic packaging, resulting in uniform cobalt de
posits. Cao Wei [9] studied the adsorption behavior of three additives
glutamic acid (DMG), 3-mercaptoacetic acid (SPS), and histidine (HIS)
on the cathode surface during cobalt electrodeposition. The result
indicate that the adsorption sites during cobalt electrodeposition ar
provided by functional groups such as the imine group of DMG, the
sulfonic acid group of SPS, and the imidazole group of HIS. However, th
actual effects of these three additives need further research. Compare
to accelerators, inhibitors play a more critical role in achieving
bottom-up cobalt dense super filling, However, inhibitors applied t
damascus copper interconnects are not suitable for electroplated cobal
interconnects. Therefore, in recent years, research on cobalt intercon
nect electroplating filling has mainly explored more suitable inhibitors
and proposed some quaternary ammonium salts and
nitrogen-containing derivatives as inhibitors for cobalt interconnect
electroplating [10]. For example, Hu et al. [11] studied the electrode
position of cobalt from ultra-thin cobalt seeds using two additives
dimethoxyoxime (DMG) and cyclohexanedioxime (CHD), on a silicon
blanket as a substrate. Through cyclic voltammetry, it was found that it
growth mode is consistent with the three-dimensional nucleation of
cobalt. Kiruba et al. [12] investigated the reduction process of cobalt in
acid salt solutions using but 2-acetyl-1,4-diol (butynediol) as an addi
tive. Research has found that butynediol can inhibit the reduction o

tion, butynediol activates proton reduction. Butynediol can serve as an
inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition. Ma Xiaochuan et al. [13] used
malachite green (MG) as an inhibitor for cobalt metal electrodeposition,
and the results showed that MG can be used as an inhibitor to achiev
over filling of cobalt metal in micron sized blind holes. They also found
that the cobalt metal electrodeposition in the solution after adding MG i
a three-dimensional nucleation process. Li Yaqiang et al. [14] studied
the inhibitory effect of dye molecule nitrotetrazolium chloride blue
(NBT) on cobalt, electrodeposition using different, electrochemica
methods. Confirmed the strong adsorption and inhibitory effect of NBT
on cobalt matrix, which can achieve bottom-up blind hole super filling.
Wu Yunwen et al. [15] studied the effects of three additives with un
saturated carbon bonds, 1,4-butynediol (BYD), 1,4-butenediol (BED)
and ethylene glycol (EG), on cobalt electrodeposition to reveal the po
tential mechanism of unsaturated carbon atom bonds in cobalt electro
deposition. Research has found that cobalt thin films prepared by BYD
electrodeposition have lower resistance and more compact morphology
After adding BYD, the crystal surface of the Co film changed from a
mixture of elongated ridges and particle shapes to a flat particle struc
ture. This conclusion indicates that additives can customize the orien
tation and properties of cobalt. Then, he studied another additive
phenylmethylsulfone (PMSO) [16], as the main additive for cobal
electrodeposition. The results indicate that PMSO has a strong inhibitor
effect on cobalt electrodeposition, and the sulfoxide groups in PMSO
preferentially adsorb on the cathode surface, exhibiting high chemica
reactivity. As the concentration of PMSO increases, the nucleation pro
cess of cobalt shifts from non transient nucleation to gradual nucleation
and the surface morphology of cobalt also changes from rough to dense
and flat, which can effectively fill high-quality cobalt through-silicon via
(TSV) grooves, indicating that PMSO is an effective additive for cobalt
electrodeposition. At present, most of the leveling agents used in cobalt
electroplating are polymer nitrogen-containing compounds, but these
leveling agents are prone to decomposition at high temperatures, mak
ing the electroplating process difficult to control, resulting in poor
experimental stability, which is not conducive to repeated operations,
and also leads to quality problems in the coating. However, the high
price of macromolecular compounds increases the experimental cost,
which is not conducive to the subsequent production process. For some
synthetic polymer composite leveling agents, the synthesis process is
complex, the polymer toxicity is high, and the environmental perfor-
mance is poor. Therefore, it is necessary to develop green and envi-
ronmentally friendly small molecule inhibitors to meet the needs of
cobalt super filling.

pounds can form coordination bonds with the cobalt surface or

produce effectively suppress the reduction of cobalt. The HMTA is a kind
of nitrogen-containing small molecule compounds containing methy-
lene structures, which indicates that the HMTA is a potential inhibitor
for cobalt deposition. Meanwhile, this HMTA is a stable compound that
is not easily decomposed at high temperatures. Therefore, in this work,
the HMTA molecules was selected to be as leveling agents for cobalt
interconnect electrodeposition. The electrochemical experiments
including cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV),
and galvanostatic method (GM) were first used to analyze the deposition
behavior of cobalt under HMTA leveling. The quantum chemistry
calculation and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation were used to
predict the adsorption active sites and the adsorption behavior of HMTA
molecules at the cobalt surface and the corresponding quantum chem-
istry parameters including the energy gap, electrostatic potential and
adsorption energy were calculated. The adsorption behavior of HMTA is
further confirmed by the in-situ electrochemical surface enhanced
Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS). Two printed circuit boards (PCBs) with
different aperture sizes were selected as the blind hole filling objects to
investigate the effect of HMTA on the filling ability of cobalt in blind
hole filling. The nucleation process of cobalt in blind holes and bottom
regions were analyzed through timed current experiments. In addition,
the effect of HMTA on the surface morphology and crystal structure of
filled cobalt was also analyzed .

2.2. Theoretical calculations
2.2.1. Quantum chemical calculations
Device Studio software was used to construct the molecular model of
the additive and then the density functional theory optimization of
HMTA was carried out by using density functional theory (DFT) method,
BDF module and water as a solvent [22,23]. Frequency calculations are
carried out at the same theoretical level to ensure that all structures are
true minima on the potential energy surface. After optimization, the
energy density distribution and electrostatic potential (ESP) of the
frontier orbits (HOMO and LUMO) were detected visually, and the en-
ergy gap was calculated by the formula. All quantum chemistry calcu-
lations use device studio’s BDF module.
2.2.2. Molecular dynamics simulation
The Forcite module in Material Studio (MS) 2023 is used to simulate
the interaction between the additive and the (100) crystal plane of co
balt in MD . The adsorption free energy between Leveler and the (100)
crystal plane was calculated in a simulation box with periodic boundary
conditions. The simulation box consists of one leveled molecule, 500
water molecules and eight layers of cobalt, which remain“Frozen” in situ
to ensure free interaction between adsorbent molecules and metal sur-
face. The Universal Force Field (UFF) uses a combination of ab initio
calculations and empirical methods to calculate the parameters in the
field, to accurately describe the interactions between molecules, and has
been used to predict the chemical property of various molecules or
compounds. UFF is used in simulation, temperature is fixed at 298 K,
NVT ensemble is used, step length is set at 0.5 fs, simulation time is 200
ps. The adsorption energy between the cobalt layer and the leveling
agent E<sub>Co-leveling</sub> <sub>agent</sub> is calculated from the following equation [24].
\mathrm{E} _ {\text { Co - leveling   agent }} = \mathrm{E} _ {\text { complex }} - \mathrm{E} _ {\text { Co }} - \mathrm{E} _ {\text { leveler }}
Ecomplex is the total energy of surface, leveling agent and interac-
tion between surface and leveling agent, and Eleveler is the energy of
cobalt crystal and free leveling agent, respectively.

3.6. Surface roughness analysis
Fig. 12 shows the surface morphology of cobalt obtained from the
electrolyte with the MPS and the electrolyte with the MPS and HMTA.
From Fig. 12a and 12c, it can be seen that the cobalt coating obtained
from the 14 ppm MPS plating solution exhibits an uneven structure, and
the surface of the coating is relatively rough. From Fig. 12b and 12d, it
can be seen that after adding 13 ppm HMTA molecules to the electro-
plating solution containing 14 ppm MPS, the cobalt layer obtained be-
comes flatter, the cobalt grain size on the coating surface is the smallest,
and the coating is smooth and flat in the macroscopic state. This in-
dicates that adding leveling agent HMTA molecules to the plating so-
lution can improve the smoothness and flatness of cobalt coatings.
3.7. Surface roughness analysis
The surface roughness of cobalt coating obtained from the electrolyte
containing MPS and that containing MPS and HMTA were analyzed
using atomic force microscopy (AFM) and the corresponding results are
shown in Fig. 13. The surface roughness of cobalt coating attained from
the electrolyte with the addition of 14 ppm MPS decreased, as shown in
Fig. 13a, its average roughness (Ra) and root mean square (RMS)
roughness (Rq) were about 4.00 nm and 4.90 nm, respectively. While for
the electrolyte containing the 13 ppm HMTA, the coating obtained ex-
hibits a minimum roughness with the Ra of about 2.41 nm and Rq of
about 3.19 nm, as shown in Fig. 13b. This means that adding HMTA can
effectively reduce the surface roughness of cobalt coatings, thereby
improving the surface smoothness of cobalt coatings.
3.8. Structural analysis
In order to explain the effect of the leveling agent HMTA on the
crystalline structure of electrodeposited cobalt with HMTA, the crys-
talline structure of the cobalt layer under different electrolytes were also
analyzed by XRD and the corresponding results are shown in Fig. 14. The
crystal planes of the cobalt layer obtained in the electrolyte containing
14 ppm MPS are (110), (101), and (110). On this basis, the crystal planes
of the cobalt layer obtained by adding 13 ppm HMTA molecules are
(100), (002), and (101). From the Fig. 14, it can be seen that compared
with the electrolyte containing 14 ppm MPS, the cobalt coating with 13
ppm HMTA molecules showed a decrease in diffraction peak intensity at
the (100) crystal plane at 41.27◦ and the (110) crystal plane at 75.73◦,
while the diffraction peak intensity related to the (002) crystal plane at
44.04◦ increased. This indicates that the leveling agent HMTA can
inhibit the growth of (100) and (100) crystal planes, and preferentially
promote the formation of cobalt crystals along the (002) crystal plane. In
summary, the homogenization behavior of HMTA on cobalt surfaces is
not only related to the inhibition of cobalt deposition by HMTA, but also
to the preferred orientation of cobalt crystal surfaces. The addition of
HMTA leads to a change in the favorable direction for the growth of
cobalt coatings.
4. Conclusion
In conclusion, a small molecule HMTA with nitrogen-containing
methylene structure was selected as leveling agent to study the depo-
sition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of cobalt under the action
of the HMTA molecules. The addition of HMTA molecule has a strong
inhibitory effect on the deposition of cobalt during electrodeposition. It
is revealed that the methylene group in the HMTA molecule belongs to
the nucleophilic group, which provides the preferred adsorption reac-
tion active site for the interaction with the cobalt surface and then
produces a strong inhibitory effect of cobalt electrodeposition. Under
the synergy of this HMTA molecule, a bottom-up super-filling behavior
is achieved during the filling process of cobalt electroplating in blind
holes. Such super-filling behavior is mainly related to the fact that the

HMTA leads to a change in the favorable direction for the growth of

4. Conclusion
In conclusion, a small molecule HMTA with nitrogen-containing
methylene structure was selected as leveling agent to study the depo-
sition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of cobalt under the action
of the HMTA molecules. The addition of HMTA molecule has a strong
inhibitory effect on the deposition of cobalt during electrodeposition. It
is revealed that the methylene group in the HMTA molecule belongs to
the nucleophilic group, which provides the preferred adsorption reac-
tion active site for the interaction with the cobalt surface and then
produces a strong inhibitory effect of cobalt electrodeposition. Under
the synergy of this HMTA molecule, a bottom-up super-filling behavior
is achieved during the filling process of cobalt electroplating in blind
holes. Such super-filling behavior is mainly related to the fact that the
